title: Troubleshooting Stuck Blades on Multi‑Blade Herb Shears
keyword: stuck blades on herb shears troubleshooting
meta_description: Blades jamming on your herb scissors? Learn how to fix and prevent stuck blades on herb shears troubleshooting guide for a smoother kitchen experience.
html:
There is nothing quite like the efficiency of a multi-blade shear when you have a mountain of cilantro or a bunch of chives to prep. But as any home cook knows, those five parallel blades can occasionally decide to stop sliding. Whether it's a stubborn piece of stem or a buildup of sticky sap, dealing with stuck blades on herb shears troubleshooting is a common part of owning these tools.

When your shears jam, the instinct is to force them open or closed. Resist that urge. Forcing a jammed blade can bend the metal or strip the pivot screw, turning a five-minute fix into a trip to the trash can. Instead, use these practical methods to get your tools gliding again.

Identifying the Cause of the Jam

Before you reach for the tools, look closely at the blades. Most jams are caused by one of three things: organic debris, misalignment, or lack of lubrication. Organic debris is the most common culprit; a tiny, fibrous piece of rosemary or a thick basil stem can wedge itself deep into the pivot point or between the blades.

Misalignment usually happens if the shears were dropped or stored under heavy pots in a drawer. If the blades aren't perfectly parallel, they'll rub against each other, creating friction that feels like a jam. Finally, if you've put your shears through the dishwasher multiple times, the factory lubricant has likely washed away, leaving the metal to grind.

Step-by-Step Stuck Blades on Herb Shears Troubleshooting

If your shears are currently frozen, follow this sequence to clear the blockage without damaging the blades:

  • The Soak: Place the shears in a bowl of warm, soapy water for 10 minutes. This softens dried plant resins and sugars that act like glue between the blades.
  • The Comb Method: If you are using the Herb Scissors (the version that comes with a cleaning comb), use that comb immediately. Slide it through the blades to push out trapped fibers. If you don't have a comb, a sturdy toothpick or a needle works well to pick out debris from the pivot.
  • The Gentle Wiggle: Instead of pulling the handles straight apart, try a slight side-to-side twisting motion while gently applying pressure. This helps dislodge wedged stems.
  • The Flush: Run a high-pressure stream of water through the blades from the back to push debris forward and out.

How to Prevent Future Blade Jams

Prevention is much easier than troubleshooting. To keep your Herb Scissors moving smoothly, change how you prep your greens. Avoid cutting through thick, woody stems (like the main stalk of a rosemary bush). These are too dense for multi-blade shears and are the primary cause of jams.

Another pro tip is to avoid the dishwasher. While many are labeled as dishwasher safe, the high heat and harsh detergents can corrode the pivot point and strip away necessary oils. A quick hand-wash with a brush and a towel-dry is all you need. If you notice the action feeling "crunchy," a single drop of food-grade mineral oil on the pivot screw will restore that buttery smooth feel.

Maintaining Your Multi-Blade Shears

Long-term maintenance ensures your mince stays consistent. Every few months, check the tightness of the center screw. If it's too loose, the blades will wobble and jam; if it's too tight, they won't close fully. Use a small screwdriver to find the "sweet spot" where the blades move freely but remain aligned.

When using the Herb Scissors, make the cleaning comb a part of your routine. Don't wait until the shears are stuck to use it. Run the comb through the blades after every single use. This prevents the buildup of "green gunk"—that compressed layer of herb residue—that eventually leads to a total jam.

When to Replace Your Shears

While most jams are fixable, some damage is permanent. If you see a visible bend in one of the five blades, or if the metal has pitted due to rust, it's time for a new pair. A bent blade will never align correctly, and you'll find yourself in a cycle of constant stuck blades on herb shears troubleshooting that isn't worth your time.

Investing in a quality set with a dedicated cleaning tool makes a world of difference. When the blades are high-carbon stainless steel and the pivot is secure, these tools become a staple of your mise en place rather than a frustration.

FAQ

Can I use WD-40 to unstick my herb shears?

No. WD-40 is not food-safe. If you need to lubricate your shears, use a small amount of food-grade mineral oil or a tiny bit of vegetable oil. These are safe for contact with your food and will effectively reduce friction.

Why do my shears jam more with basil than with parsley?

Basil contains more sticky resins and oils than parsley. These oils act as an adhesive, trapping small particles of leaf and stem against the metal. This is why using the cleaning comb frequently is especially important when working with "sticky" herbs.

Will putting my shears in the freezer help unstick them?

Generally, no. Cold temperatures cause metal to contract, which can actually make a tight jam feel more secure. Warm, soapy water is always the better first step to break down the organic material causing the blockage.
